The ruan is a traditional plucked instrument from China, a chordophone, also called ruanqin or ruanxian. It is built with a round soundbox, a fretted neck and four strings; the modern ruan usually has twenty-four frets and steel strings, and by range it is divided into soprano, small, alto, tenor and bass ruan, with a bowed ruan as well. It is usually played sitting down, the body on the thigh, the left hand stopping the strings and the right hand plucking with a pick or with false nails; the pick gives a clearer tone and false nails suit multi-part solos. The ruan is common in Chinese opera and in the plucked section of the Chinese orchestra, where the alto and tenor ruan mostly fill the middle and low register, the soprano ruan can sometimes replace the liuqin, and it also appears in ruan ensembles and solos.
阮源於中國，前身可追溯至秦漢時期圓形直項撥弦樂器，漢代文獻稱琵琶或秦琵琶，起源約: The ruan comes from China, its forerunner a round-bodied, straight-necked plucked instrument of the Qin and Han periods; Han texts call it pipa or qin pipa, and its origin is roughly 217 to 105 BC. In the Tang, when the curved-neck pipa arrived, the round-bodied straight-necked instrument was renamed ruanxian, after Ruan Xian of the Western Jin; in the time of Wu Zetian a bronze ruanxian with 13 frets and a round soundbox was unearthed from a Sichuan tomb. In the Tang it reached Japan, where it survives in the Shōsōin. After the twentieth century steel strings were adopted; in the 1950s the People's Republic of China developed it into a four-string, 24-fret instrument with a larger soundbox, dividing it after the violin family into soprano, small, alto, tenor and bass ruan; in 1987 Liu Xing's Yunnan Memories established the alto ruan as a solo instrument in the Chinese orchestra.
阮為中國弦鳴撥弦樂器，圓形共鳴箱配四弦與高品，音色柔和，低音域沉穩。以右手撥片或: The ruan is a Chinese plucked chordophone with a round soundbox, four strings and many frets, a soft timbre and a steady low register. The right hand's pick or false nails control volume and clarity. The modern twenty-four frets extend the range beyond the old thirteen, and each instrument in the family, from soprano to bass, has its own tuning, covering a wide range. The pick gives a louder, clearer tone, false nails suit multi-part solos better, and metal frets are brighter than ivory ones. The alto and tenor ruan are common in the plucked section of the Chinese orchestra, filling the middle and low register, and the soprano ruan sometimes replaces the liuqin.
阮為坐姿演奏，琴身置於大腿上並抱於胸前，左手按弦，右手以撥片觸弦發聲；早期亦用兩: The ruan is played sitting down, the body on the thigh and held against the chest, the left hand stopping the strings and the right hand touching them with a pick; early players also used two or five acrylic false nails, and today the string tension usually means a pick. A beginner can first tune according to the size, then sound the strings with the basic right-hand strokes such as tan and tiao, while the left hand adds stopping techniques such as harmonics, glissando and vibrato. Methods differ between schools, so it is best to begin with a steady hold, the angle of the pick and coordination between the hands.
阮為弦鳴撥弦樂器，現代琴身材質來源未載明；古代阮咸以紫檀製成並鑲螺鈿。弦早期為絲: The ruan is a plucked chordophone; the source does not state the materials of the modern body, while the ancient ruanxian was made of rosewood and inlaid with mother-of-pearl. The strings were silk at first and steel after the twentieth century, with the bass strings flat-wound. The frets are commonly ivory or, in recent times, metal set into wood. The pick was formerly horn and is now mostly plastic or nylon; the nail technique uses acrylic false nails fixed with tape.
阮的聆聽示範可從中國戲曲與中國管弦樂團的彈撥聲部入手；中阮、大阮常填補男高音與低: Listening to the ruan can start from Chinese opera and the plucked section of the Chinese orchestra; the alto and tenor ruan often fill the tenor and bass, and the soprano ruan sometimes replaces the liuqin. Liu Xing's Yunnan Memories lets you hear the alto ruan as a concerto soloist. There are also ruan ensembles of small, alto and tenor ruan, where you can hear several parts. The bowed ruan and the large bowed ruan stand in for the gehu and bass gehu in large Chinese orchestras, with a range close to the cello and double bass.
